analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations and unions run political ads naming candidates without disclosing the spending.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote; it sat in the Rules Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would roll back three key parts of the 2002 campaign finance law (known as McCain-Feingold). It would end the requirement that groups disclose their spending on 'electioneering communications' — ads that mention a federal candidate shortly before an election. It would lift the ban on corporations and labor unions paying for those ads out of their general treasuries. And it would stop treating ads coordinated with a candidate's campaign as campaign contributions subject to contribution limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and labor unions, which could spend unlimited treasury money on ads attacking or supporting candidates without ever telling the public who paid. Candidates and parties also gain a loophole: an ad 'coordinated' with their campaign would no longer count as a contribution they must report. Political ad buyers and the media outlets that sell the ad time also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, unions, and big ad spenders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the disclosure requirement for electioneering communications, so no person would have to file reports with the Federal Election Commission about disbursements for candidate-naming ads made on or after November 6, 2002.

Repeals the ban on corporations and labor organizations making disbursements for electioneering communications, allowing them to fund these ads directly from general treasury funds rather than regulated political committees.

Removes the provision treating coordinated communications as contributions, so ads secretly planned with a candidate's campaign would no longer be subject to campaign contribution limits and reporting.
The changes take effect retroactively, as if included in the original 2002 Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act, erasing the reporting record for spending since November 2002.

analysis.who_pays: Voters, who would lose the ability to see who is paying for last-minute political ads and would face a flood of undisclosed corporate and union money in elections. Candidates would also face attack ads from hidden funders they cannot trace or respond to.

drawbacks.text: Ending disclosure entirely — rather than just lowering limits — would let corporations and unions bankroll candidate-naming ads in secret, so voters could not judge who is behind a political message.

Because the bill applies retroactively to all spending since November 6, 2002, it would wipe out required reporting records that already exist, permanently hiding past spending rather than only changing future rules.

By removing coordinated-communication rules, it would open a path around contribution limits: a wealthy backer could fund ads planned with a candidate's own campaign without those amounts counting as contributions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a genuine benefit to its backers — more freedom for corporations and unions to speak about candidates — but it achieves this by removing disclosure, not just limits, and it applies retroactively to erase existing records. The cost falls on voters' ability to know who funds political advertising in the final weeks of elections, which is exactly the information the 2002 law was written to protect. The design is broad enough that even readers sympathetic to deregulation have reason to balk at the retroactive erasure of disclosure records.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2004 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chambliss introduced the bill on July 21, 2004, joined by Republican Sens. Inhofe, Allen, and Lott as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over election law.
No further action was ever taken — the committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voters kept the disclosure rules and corporate-spending limits of the 2002 campaign finance law, because the bill never advanced. The corporations and unions that stood to gain unlimited, undisclosed ad spending got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voters who kept campaign disclosure rules

for.name: Sen. Saxby Chambliss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. James Inhofe, George Allen, and Trent Lott

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no vote was ever taken, so the full chamber's partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would let corporations spend general treasury money on ads that name candidates, with no public disclosure of the spending. Voters would lose the ability to see who is paying for last-minute political messages.

Unions would gain the same freed-up right to fund candidate-naming ads from general funds. Union political spending is at least traceable to a known institution, but the disclosure repeal would hide it too.
Loosening limits on electioneering communications would likely increase demand for political ad time, a revenue gain for media sellers. Their gain tracks volume of spending, whichever side buys it.
